draft.title: Secondary data
card: Secondary data is information that someone else collected for their own purpose. Geographers use it when they did not gather it themselves.
Common sources include census figures, climate records from the Bureau of Meteorology, government reports and published maps.
It can cover large areas or long periods that one student could not study alone. It may not match the exact question being asked.
Check how reliable it is. Ask who collected it, when, how and why. A recent source from a trusted body with a clear method is more reliable.
draft.remember: Secondary data is collected by others, so check its source, date and purpose before using it.

a.q: Which of these is secondary data for a study of rainfall in Broken Hill?
opts: Rainfall records published by a weather agency
Rain gauge readings taken by the student at the site
A student's field sketch of a dry creek bed
Answers from a survey the student gave to locals
a.why: The weather agency collected the records, not the student, so they are secondary data. The gauge readings, sketch and survey were all gathered first-hand by the student, so the tempting gauge option is still not secondary.
a.clue: Who collected the data in the first place?

b.q: Ava is studying population change in Wagga Wagga. She finds a table of figures on a website with no author, no date and no method. What is the best reason to be careful using it?
opts: Its source, date and method cannot be checked
It was collected by someone other than Ava
It covers a larger area than she could study alone
It is a table, not a map or graph
b.why: Reliability depends on knowing who collected the data, when and how. Here none of this can be checked. Being collected by others is true of all secondary data, so that does not make it unreliable.
b.clue: All secondary data comes from others. What is missing here that lets you judge it?

a.best: Rainfall records published by a weather agency

b.best: Its source, date and method cannot be checked
